- **(Resumed)** Finish the opus application and continue the deep-dive queue

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **join.com dedupe**: shows "You've applied on <date>" on already-sent roles — free deduplication. Caught Tangible and CityZ. Its metadata lies about freshness (Novosafe said "updated 12 August", live page said "archived 6 months ago"; SERA same).
- **Greenhouse stale-CV trap**: autofills older `Prabhavit_CV-.pdf` from MyGreenhouse. Must click X and re-upload every time.
- **Greenhouse closed-posting signature**: a posting URL serving the board index (often with `?error=true`) means the role is CLOSED.
- **Ashby location-combobox overwrite**: after selecting an option, typing again silently overwrites it. Set "Itasy, Madagascar" at Hexa. Fix: triple_click, retype, click exact option, screenshot-verify.
- **Ashby is NOT uniformly a JS shell** — n8n's FDE posting and Vapi's rendered fine while board indexes didn't.
- **Phone country prefix bug**: typing "+39 351..." into a field showing "+39" produces "+39003516107807". Recruitee/Greenhouse default to company country — switch selector first, type bare number.
- **File input is the element typed `file`**, not the visible "Attach" button.
- **Aggregator mirrors are not verification**: RemoteRocketship, Himalayas, Jobgether, Built In, Remotive were wrong repeatedly. ~50% attrition is normal.
- **WebSearch session budget = 200 calls**; exhausted. WebFetch has a PROVENANCE_REQUIRED restriction (only URLs from user messages or prior search/fetch results).
- **Rate limits**: n8n 1 per 15 days (applied 5 Aug → clear 20 Aug); Camunda 2/30 days; Siena AI 3/60 days; Scale AI 90 days; ElevenLabs hard throttle.
- **Letter generator**: `python3 make_letter.py --in x.json --out "X_Motivation_Letter.pdf"` with keys `role`, `location`, `date`, `opening`, `role_specific`, `closing`.
- **Bash `cd` does not persist between calls.**

**Lleverage "describe a project" — USER-FLAGGED.** I answered "Describe a project that best demonstrates your technical abilities" with the FlowSpace migration and then appended a paragraph about the Dutch work permit and Directive 2003/109/EC. It reads as though the answer to a technical question is visa admin. **Recruitee cannot be edited after submitting.** User said: *"describe a project, you asnwered wrong"*. Logged as CORRECTION; new rule added: every answer stays on the question asked, eligibility notes go in the cover letter or a dedicated field only.

Neither is established, and the second contradicts his Italian being beginner level. Rewritten from known facts only (no CS degree, BA at 97/110, self-taught, FlowSpace takeover). Recorded as: *inferring biographical colour is the most likely way to put a lie in front of an employer.*

**Ashby combobox at Hexa**: LinkedIn URL landed in the still-open location field, resolving to "Itasy, Madagascar". Caught on screenshot; triple_click, retyped "Venice, Italy", clicked the exact option.

**Phone defaults**: Spyrosoft defaulted +48 Poland; BAS Group, Freeday, Lleverage defaulted Netherlands. Fixed by switching the country selector before typing the bare number.

**Duvo radio misclick**: selected "Word of mouth" instead of "Other". Corrected before submitting.

**Salary rule contradiction discovered**: `rules_out.md` (6 Aug) says *"Do NOT anchor on the posting's own published band, his explicit instruction. Quote his number, not theirs."* The 12 Aug instruction reverses this. Documented that 12 Aug supersedes.

**Deep-sweep agents failed entirely**: WebSearch returned `this session has used its web search budget (200 of 200)`; WebFetch returned `PROVENANCE_REQUIRED`. Reported honestly as "untouched, not empty" rather than letting silence imply the slice was swept.

Plus: he sells to product companies who see 8-companies-in-3-years as a liability rather than consultancies who see it as an asset; and the GitHub gap.
- **Coworking/proptech confirmed effectively dead** — OfficeRnD zero listings, Nexudus none, Robin 404, deskbird/Kadence no EU engineering.

Use prabhavitg@gmail.com, NOT spaces@flowspace.co. Nothing counts as submitted without on-screen confirmation. No em dashes anywhere. # Prabhavit's motivation letter — the real one, and how to adapt it

2026). It is the voice to match and the structure to reuse. Keep his sentences where they still
fit; change the opening, the role-specific paragraph, and the closing.

## Layout

```

Venice, Italy +39 3516107807 | prabhavitg@gmail.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/prabhavit

<date>
```

2. **The role-specific paragraph.** Mirror the actual requirements in the posting against things he has built, using their vocabulary where it's honest to do so.
3. **The closing line.** One sentence, tuned to what the role is about.

Keep it to one page. His original is one page and it works.

# Standing rules for submitting applications on Prabhavit's behalf

These are his instructions, not suggestions, and several of them exist because they were got
wrong once already. Read this file before touching a single form. If a rule here conflicts with
your own judgement about what would "look better" to an employer, the rule wins — it's his
career and his call.

## The non-negotiables

1. **Attach the CV to every application. Never submit one without it.** Use only the CV file he
   most recently supplied — the exact PDF, unmodified. Do not regenerate it, reformat it, or
   substitute a version you made. If the file isn't available in this session, stop and ask;
   don't proceed with a CV-less application.

1b. **Write bespoke material ONLY for low-match roles (his instruction, 12 Aug 2026).** If the role is a
   strong match, send the CV and keep free-text answers short — **he writes those cover letters himself.**
   Do not generate one. If a strong-match form makes the cover letter *required*, submit nothing and hand
   it to him with the link. Reserve letters and long written answers for roles where there is a real gap
   that needs explaining. Do not generate a letter by reflex.

1c. **Keep each answer to the question that was asked.** Work-authorisation, relocation and availability
   notes go in the cover letter or a dedicated eligibility field — NEVER appended to a technical question
   like "describe a project". He flagged this after it happened on the Lleverage form.

2. **Salary or rate expectation: €40,000–50,000 baseline (updated 12 Aug 2026).** Where the posting **discloses a band**, do not quote below it — align to their number instead (e.g. a posting at €70–120k gets an answer inside that band, not €50,000). He set this himself after seeing that his old €30–40k was under every disclosed band in the market. Write it plainly — "€30,000–40,000" or
   "EUR 30,000–40,000, negotiable" at most. **Do not** pad it with explanations about market
   bands, do not substitute a higher figure because the posting advertises more, and do not
   write a paragraph where a number was asked for. If you think his number is low, say so once
   in chat and then use his number anyway.

3. **Never leave a cover letter field blank when one is asked for.** Adapt his motivation letter
   (`assets/motivation-letter.md`) to the specific role. Where the form takes a file, generate a
   PDF; where it takes text, paste the adapted body.

   **This includes cover-letter fields that are not marked required.** An optional "Cover Letter —
   Attach / Dropbox / Enter manually" block on a Greenhouse form still counts as being asked. This
   rule was broken once by exactly that reading: the letter had already been written and the field
   was skipped because the form would submit without it. Once submitted, there is no going back —
   Greenhouse and Ashby don't let an application be edited — so the cost of missing it is a
   permanent gap in an application he can't re-send.

4. **When a form asks for years of experience and wants 3 or more, write 3.** Don't skip an
   application because a year count is above his. Answer honestly with 3 and let the employer
   decide. Same principle for any "do you have N years of X" free-text field: give the true
   number and one clause of context, no more.

5. **Skip join.com** unless he has signed in on that browser. Their apply flow forces account
   creation or Google sign-in, and account creation is off-limits.

6. **Don't make the writing sound AI-generated.** Details in the writing section below.

- *Legally eligible to work where you'll work from?* → **Yes**
- *Which status allows you to work there?* → **citizen / permanent resident** (the EU long-term permit)
- *Will you require sponsorship now or in future?* → **No** for EU-based and remote-from-Italy roles. For a **UK, Swiss or US** role, the honest answer is **Yes** — answer it truthfully and flag the role to him rather than fudging it.
- *Able and willing to work remotely?* → **Yes**
- *Based in Europe?* → **Yes**
- *Previously worked in a customer-facing capacity?* → **Yes** (FlowSpace: mediated between the internal team, an external agency and members; Urlink: project manager on client requirements)
- *Production experience at a large enterprise (1,000+)?* → **"only shipped in smaller companies or startups"** — true, don't inflate it
- *AI agents / agentic workflows?* → **"built and operated agentic systems in production, including testing for non-determinism and failure recovery"** — true, and his strongest answer on any form
- *BPMN specifically?* → he has n8n workflow automation in production but no BPMN. Pick the middle option where one exists; never claim BPMN production experience
- *Native English speaker?* → **No, fluent at C2 level**
- *Pronouns, gender, ethnicity, disability, veteran status* → leave blank or "prefer not to say". Never guess demographic data.
- *How did you hear about us?* → the honest answer is a job board; pick "Job Board" / "Other" and say "job board" if a follow-up field appears.

## Writing that doesn't read as machine-written

His own motivation letter is the voice to match: direct, concrete, slightly formal, first person,
specific numbers, no salesmanship. Things to avoid because they are the tells:

- Openings like "I'm excited to apply" or "I am thrilled by the opportunity".
- Three-item lists everywhere, and sentences of identical length stacked together.
- "Leverage", "passionate about", "cutting-edge", "seamlessly", "robust solutions", "I thrive in".
- Restating the job description back at them instead of saying what he did.
- Perfect symmetry. Real writing has a short sentence after a long one, and occasionally starts with "But" or "So".

What to do instead: name the specific thing he built, the tool he built it in, and the number it
moved. Say plainly where he's weaker rather than papering over it — a sentence like "my agent work
has been in n8n rather than a Python harness, so I'd be learning your idioms early on" reads as
human and costs nothing.

## The facts worth reaching for

Use these rather than adjectives. They're all on his CV.

- FlowSpace: took over an existing system, grew the platform **2,000 → 4,500+ users**, led the migration from **Bubble.io to Next.js + Laravel** on a live product, built the support **AI agents**, lead capture and enrichment into the CRM, GTM and outbound automations, and a scraping/parsing tool that increased listings.
- Integrations shipped: **Office RnD, Nexudus** (automated bookings), Clubee API, Sendgrid, Google APIs, OpenAI/Anthropic, Eden AI.
- UltraStrategy: **CV-parsing tool in n8n + Eden AI**. Get2Germany: Google API tracking, AI tools for finding courses and jobs. Clubee: API integration, unit testing and QA.
- Urlink: built a platform largely with AI, acting as PM and developer.
- Eight European companies in about three years (UK, Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Luxembourg, Netherlands) — the ramp-fast argument.
- Certifications: Microsoft Copilot Studio Agent Academy, Microsoft AI agents, Power Automate, Tray.ai Build Practitioner.
- Degree: BA Philosophy, International Studies & Economics, Ca' Foscari Venice. No CS degree — don't hide it, don't apologise for it.

## Things you must not do

- Create an account, set a password, or sign in as him.
- Solve a CAPTCHA.
- Enter payment details, government ID numbers, or a date of birth he hasn't given.
- Invent a GitHub link, a portfolio URL, a referral name, or demographic data.
- Claim experience he can't evidence — specifically BPMN, Python backend depth, ML research, or a language beyond English.
- Submit two applications to the same company for roles he clearly doesn't qualify for. One good application beats two scattershot ones.

When you hit one of these, stop that application, leave the form filled if you can, and tell him
exactly what's needed.

## Pre-submit checklist — run it before every single click of Submit

Submission is irreversible, so the last thirty seconds before it are the ones that matter. Take a
screenshot of the whole form, scroll through it, and confirm each line:

1. **CV attached?** The filename is visible in the upload box, not just "Upload File".
2. **Cover letter / motivation letter field present anywhere on this form?** If yes — required or
   not — it is filled. Search the page text for "cover letter", "motivation", "letter" before
   deciding it isn't there.
3. **Every field with a `*` has a value**, including the ones that only appear after another
   answer is chosen, and the ones that re-blank themselves silently (Greenhouse phone-country and
   city pickers do this).
4. **Salary or rate says his number**, short, in the currency the field expects.
5. **Nothing invented** — no GitHub link, referral, or demographic answer he didn't give.
6. **Name, email and phone actually registered**, not just visible. Ashby will claim a filled field
   is missing; retype by keystroke when it does.

Then submit, and confirm the success page before you call it done.

## Log every submission

After each one, record: company, role, the ATS, what was entered in each non-obvious field, the
confirmation text you actually saw, and the link. If you didn't see a confirmation, it didn't
happen — say so. He is tracking this in a spreadsheet and a silent failure is worse than a
visible one.

# Candidate profile — Prabhavit Gupta

This file is the definition of "good fit". Read it before every search. If Prabhavit
corrects something about what he wants (pay, location, seniority, a company he'd never
join), update this file so the next run inherits it — a search that keeps re-learning his
preferences from scratch wastes his time.

Last updated: 2026-08-05, from `Prabhavit_CV.pdf` plus his stated preferences.

## Snapshot

- AI Solutions & Automation Engineer / Lead Developer. ~3 years professional (mid-2023 → now), entirely in European startups.
- Based in **Venice, Italy**. Contact: prabhavitg@gmail.com, +39 351 610 7807.
- **European Long Term Residence Permit — no EU sponsorship required.** Treat this as a selling point, not a constraint: postings that say "must have existing EU work authorization" or "we cannot sponsor" are *open* to him, and that requirement removes most of his competition.
- Most recent role: Lead Developer (full-time, freelance) at **FlowSpace.co** (London, remote), Mar 2024 – Jul 2026. That contract has just ended, so he is **available now** — posting freshness matters.
- BA Philosophy, International Studies & Economics, minor in Entrepreneurship — Ca' Foscari University of Venice, 2020–2024. **No CS degree.**
- Languages: Hindi (native), English (professional), Italian (beginner).

## Scope of the search

Two things widen this beyond a plain EU employee search, and both change what counts as a hit:

**1. Geography — worldwide, prioritised by how workable it is from Venice.**

- **Tier 1 — workable from Italy today:** fully remote roles open to Europe/EMEA/worldwide, plus anything remote-within-Italy or on-site in Venice/Milan. No permits, no move. This is the bulk of every shortlist.
- **Tier 2 — non-EU Europe, remote:** UK, Switzerland, Norway companies hiring remotely across Europe. Same practical story as Tier 1; note that his EU permit does **not** cover UK/CH employment on-site.
- **Tier 3 — relocation or sponsorship needed:** US, Canada, UAE/Gulf, Singapore, Australia, or an EU country requiring an on-site move. Include these when the match is genuinely strong, flag them `Relocation` or `Sponsorship` in Watch-outs, and keep them a minority of the sheet — they are slower, lower-probability applications, not filler.

**2. Work basis — employment and contracting both count.**

He has worked freelance/contract for most of his career (FlowSpace, Urlink, UltraStrategy, Qomodo, Clubee were all freelance or collaborator engagements), so contract work is not a fallback for him — it's his normal mode.

- Include: contract, freelance, B2B, fixed-term, day-rate, project-based, fractional, part-time, contract-to-hire.
- Contracting also unlocks companies that "can't hire in Italy" — many will engage a contractor or use an employer-of-record where a payroll hire is impossible. A posting that says "US-based employees only" is worth a second look if it also mentions contractors.
- For contract roles, capture the **rate** (day rate or hourly) in the Salary column and mark the basis, so he can compare a €400/day contract against a €60k salary.
- Skip unpaid, equity-only, commission-only, and "join our talent pool" listings with no live engagement behind them.

## Target titles, in priority order

**Track A — AI / automation engineering** (what he already does, highest hit rate)
AI Solutions Engineer · AI Automation Engineer · AI Engineer · Automation Engineer ·
AI Implementation Engineer · LLM / Agent Engineer · Applied AI Engineer

**Track B — forward-deployed / client-facing technical**
Forward Deployed Engineer · Solutions Engineer · Solutions Architect (mid) ·
AI Implementation Consultant · Technical Delivery / Account Engineer · Sales Engineer (technical)

**Track C — product / full-stack build roles**
Full-stack Engineer (TypeScript, Next.js, Laravel) · Product Engineer ·
Founding Engineer (small team) · Low-code / Rapid Prototyping Engineer · Automation Consultant

**Track D — technical product**
Technical Product Manager · AI Product Manager / Product Owner · Product Operations (technical)

Tracks A and B convert best. Include C and D, but weight them slightly lower unless the
posting explicitly values AI/automation experience or hands-on prototyping.

## What he can evidence in an interview

Match job requirements against these, not against generic "AI experience":

- **Shipped AI agents in production**: customer-support agents, data-scraping/parsing tools that grew platform listings, a CV-parsing tool (n8n + Eden AI).
- **Scale/impact number**: took FlowSpace from 2,000 → 4,500+ users through iterative product work.
- **Platform migration ownership**: led migration of a live product from Bubble.io to Next.js + Laravel.
- **API integration depth**: Office RnD, Nexudus, CRM lead-capture integrations, Sendgrid, Google APIs, Clubee API, OpenAI/ChatGPT, Eden AI.
- **GTM / revenue-adjacent automation**: sales-funnel automations, lead enrichment, outbound — unusual for an engineer and a strong signal for forward-deployed and solutions roles.
- **Product ownership**: business-logic documentation, coordinating an external agency, mediating between internal team and agency, QA.
- **Breadth across 8 European companies** (UK, Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Luxembourg, Netherlands) — he ramps on new codebases and contexts fast, which is exactly the contractor pitch.

## Stack keywords worth searching on

`n8n` · `AI agents` · `LLM` · `RAG` · `prompt engineering` · `OpenAI API` · `Claude Code` ·
`automation` · `workflow automation` · `TypeScript` · `Next.js` · `Laravel` · `Supabase` ·
`Playwright` · `Bubble.io` · `low-code` · `no-code` · `API integration` · `Zapier / Make / Tray.ai` ·
`Microsoft Copilot Studio` · `Power Automate` · `chatbot` · `QA automation`

`n8n`, `AI agents` and `low-code` are his sharpest differentiators — companies hiring
"automation engineers" often name these tools explicitly, and those postings are far less
crowded than generic "AI Engineer" listings.

## Seniority band

- Target **mid-level**: 2–5 years required experience, or postings that state no year count.
- "Senior" is worth including when the requirement is ~4–5 years and the stack matches well; he holds lead-level responsibility even with a modest year count.
- Drop **Staff / Principal / Head of / Director / Lead (people-management)** and anything asking 7+ years.
- Junior/graduate roles are a step backwards from Lead Developer; include only if the company is exceptional (frontier AI lab, well-known scale-up) or the pay is unusually strong.
- Contract roles are less year-count sensitive — judge them on whether he could deliver the scope of work, which is often clearer than the seniority label.

## Hard gates — drop the role if any of these are true

1. **Requires professional fluency in a language he doesn't speak** — most often Italian (beginner), German, French, Dutch, Spanish. English-only requirements are fine.
2. **Deep specialist requirements he cannot evidence**: ML research / publications / PhD, training or fine-tuning foundation models from scratch, CUDA/GPU kernel work, distributed-systems SRE at scale, mobile-native (Swift/Kotlin), heavy data engineering (Spark/dbt/Airflow).
3. **Staffing agency, body shop, or aggregator repost with no named end client**, and outsourcing firms advertising "remote Europe" that are really India/LATAM delivery centres (common on Lever — verify the entity before trusting it).
4. **Unpaid, equity-only, commission-only, or a talent-pool listing** with no actual open engagement.
5. **Closed, expired, or unverifiable posting** — see the verification step in SKILL.md.

Note what is *not* a hard gate any more: being outside the EU, needing sponsorship, or
requiring relocation. Those become Tier 3 with a flag. A US-only or APAC-only role that
cannot engage a contractor abroad and won't relocate him is still a drop — but say so
because the posting rules him out, not because of where the company sits.

## Preferences (score adjustments, not gates)

Better fit:
- Fully remote with an explicit Europe/EMEA/worldwide eligibility statement.
- Startups and scale-ups (roughly 10–300 people) where one person owns a problem end to end.
- Companies whose product *is* AI/automation/agents, or whose operations are automation-heavy.
- Postings that value shipping and portfolio over credentials — "CS degree required" converts poorly for him even where he could do the work.
- Contract engagements with a defined scope and a stated rate.
- Salary or rate disclosed. Disclosure is a mild positive signal on top of the number itself.
- Posted within the last 30 days; within 7 days is materially better.

Worse fit:
- Big-corporate, heavy-process environments and long enterprise hiring loops.
- Timezone requirements demanding full US working-hours coverage — workable for a contract, wearing for a permanent role, so flag it rather than dropping it.
- Roles that are pure maintenance of a legacy stack with no AI/automation surface.

**Salary / rate expectation:** not yet stated. Ask once, in passing, the first time it
matters, and record the answer here. Until then report what postings disclose and don't
guess at what's acceptable.

**Work basis (stated 2026-08-05):** he is **open to contractor roles as well as employment**
— neither is a fallback, so carry both in every sweep and let fit decide the ranking. A
US-based company that engages international contractors counts as **Tier 1, not Tier 3**;
only US-payroll-only postings drop out. He also asked for roles **outside the EU** to be
included, which is why geography is worldwide with tiering rather than an EU filter.

**Italy-based roles** (Venice, Milan, remote-within-Italy) are always welcome — the one case
where on-site or hybrid is a plus rather than a watch-out.

Base directory for this skill: /root/.claude/skills/synced/job-hunt

# Job hunt

Prabhavit is looking for work right now — his FlowSpace contract ended in July 2026. What
helps him is a short list of openings that are **real, currently open, and genuinely open to
him**, each with an honest reason it's worth an application. What hurts him is volume: a dead
link, a role that turns out to be US-payroll-only, or a staff-level posting he has no chance at
costs him more time than a missed opportunity does. Bias the whole process towards precision.

Two references do the heavy lifting:

- `references/candidate-profile.md` — what "good fit" means. **Read it before every sweep.** It holds his eligibility, target titles, seniority band, hard gates and preferences.
- `references/sources.md` — the tested search playbook: which domains and URL patterns actually return live postings, which are dead ends, and the specific ways postings lie. **Read it before your first search in a session.**

Don't interview him before starting. He's already told the skill what he wants; ask at most one
question, and only when the answer would change the entire sweep (for example, if he names a
company that has no public board). Otherwise run the default sweep and note your assumptions in
the reply.

## Step 1 — frame the sweep

Set five parameters before searching. Anything the request specifies overrides these defaults:

| Parameter | Default |
|---|---|
| Tracks | All four from the profile, weighted A (AI/automation) > B (forward-deployed/solutions) > C (full-stack/product) > D (technical PM) |
| Geography | Worldwide, prioritised by the eligibility tiers in the profile — mostly Tier 1, a minority of Tier 3 |
| Work basis | Employment **and** contract/freelance, in the same sheet, flagged so he can compare a day rate against a salary |
| Freshness | Posted within 30 days; prefer the last 7 |
| Size | 12–20 verified roles. Expect roughly **one in three candidates to survive verification** — dead postings, board-index degradation, false "Remote" labels — so plan on fetching 3–4× the target. If the first pass lands short, run a second discovery pass with different vocabulary rather than shipping four rows. |

A narrow request ("just contract work", "only n8n stuff", "anything at ElevenLabs") narrows the
sweep — don't pad it back out with unrelated roles to hit a count.

## Step 2 — sweep wide before filtering

Cast a much wider net than the final sheet, because most candidates die at verification. Aim for
**50+ raw candidates**; fewer than ~30 means the sweep was too narrow, and the fix is almost
always vocabulary — the same job is posted as "AI Automation Engineer", "Applied AI Engineer",
"Solutions Engineer" and "Automation Consultant" at four different companies.

Verification is what caps the size of the sheet, so spend the discovery budget in ways that make
verification cheap. **Board APIs verify a whole company in one call** (§5 of `sources.md`), so
when several candidates come from the same org, check the org once instead of fetching each
posting. Where subagents are available, give each one a source family *and* have it return
already-verified rows — parallel verification is what turns a 6-row sheet into a 15-row one.

Run these in parallel in a single message (see `sources.md` for exact syntax and templates):

1. Two or three `WebSearch` calls with `allowed_domains` on the ATS hosts — one per track.
2. One contract-vocabulary query using the literal words that work: `"contract"`, `"6-month contract"`, `freelance`, `B2B`, `part time`, `fractional`.
3. One stack-keyword query — `n8n`, `low-code`, `AI agents`, `Bubble.io`. These postings are much less crowded and are his sharpest edge.
4. Two or three board fetches — euremotejobs region paths, remoterocketship with `sort=DateAdded`, himalayas (serialize these, it rate-limits).

If subagents are available, fan the sweep out: give each agent one source family and a fixed
return shape (title, company, url, location wording, comp, posted date, basis). Verification is
fetch-heavy, so parallelising the discovery leaves budget for it. Tell each agent to use only
WebSearch/WebFetch — curl and python fetching are prohibited in this environment.

## Step 3 — filter against the profile

Apply the hard gates from `candidate-profile.md` — language requirements he can't meet, deep ML
specialisation, agencies and aggregator reposts with no named end client, unpaid or
talent-pool listings. Being outside the EU is **not** a gate any more; it moves a role to
eligibility Tier 3 with a `Relocation` or `Sponsorship` flag.

Keep a short list of notable drops and why. When the sheet comes back with 14 roles instead of
40, he should be able to see that the filter did the work rather than wondering whether the
search was lazy.

## Step 4 — verify every survivor by fetching it

He will click every link in the sheet, so every row must come from a page you actually loaded.
Never list a role from a search snippet alone, and never reconstruct a URL that looks plausible.

For each candidate:

- Normalise the URL first (strip Ashby's `?embed=js`, `/application`, `?utm_data=…`; add `?language=en` on Personio).
- Fetch it, and pull: exact title, company, the **eligibility sentence** (not the word "Remote" in the title), comp or rate if disclosed, posted date, seniority requirement, and whether it's employment or contract.
- **If a single-posting fetch comes back describing many different jobs, the posting is closed** — Greenhouse silently serves the board index for dead roles and nothing else signals it. Drop it.
- Drop anything you can't confirm is live. A quiet omission is better than a broken row.
- When a posting looks strong but the fetch is ambiguous, check the company's JSON board API (`sources.md` §5) rather than guessing.

## Step 5 — score honestly

```
Fit = role & track match        30
    + eligibility & work basis  25
    + stack overlap             20
    + seniority realism         15
    + signal quality            10
```

- **Role & track match** — how close the actual responsibilities are to what he's done, not how good the title sounds.
- **Eligibility & work basis** — Tier 1 (workable from Italy today) scores full marks; Tier 2 (non-EU Europe, remote) most of them; Tier 3 (relocation or sponsorship) a fraction. A company willing to engage a contractor abroad scores as Tier 1 even if it's US-based.
- **Stack overlap** — named tools he has shipped with beat adjacent ones. `n8n` in a JD is worth more than a generic "Python required".
- **Seniority realism** — will they actually interview someone with ~3 years and no CS degree?
- **Signal quality** — freshness, disclosed comp, company type, clear scope.

Use the range. If every role scores 82–88 the scores carry no information and he can't triage;
a real sweep produces a spread. Bands: **80+** apply this week · **65–79** solid, worth an
application · **50–64** worth a look if the top of the list dries up. Below 50, leave it out and
say why in chat if it was interesting.

## Step 6 — build the spreadsheet

Write the roles to JSON and run the bundled script — it owns the column layout, tier colours,
fit colour-scale, filters and the "Search notes" sheet, so week-to-week shortlists stay
comparable and no run has to reinvent openpyxl:

```bash
python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/build_shortlist.py --in roles.json --out "Role shortlist — 5 Aug 2026.xlsx"
```

Use the absolute path to the skill directory — the working directory during a sweep is rarely
the skill folder.

The JSON shape is documented in the script's docstring. Fill `sweep_notes` — sources swept,
queries run, raw/gated/verified counts, notable drops — because that sheet is how he judges
whether the search covered the ground. Then deliver the file with `SendUserFile`.

## Step 7 — report briefly in chat

Short and useful; the spreadsheet holds the detail. Roughly:

- One line on what was swept and what came back (`19 verified from ~60 candidates`).
- The top three, one line each: role, company, and the specific reason it fits.
- What to do first — which one or two to apply to today, and why those.
- **A market read** — the part a bare list can't give him. What the roles you saw are paying (bands, or rates for contract work), which title framings are getting posted and which have dried up, and anything about his own profile that is visibly costing him applications. The most useful example so far: the Bubble.io/no-code weighting on his CV reads as "no-code contractor" to code-first teams, which is a fixable presentation problem rather than a skills gap. Say that kind of thing plainly — a shortlist plus one true observation beats a longer shortlist.
- Where a role would be a contract engagement with a non-EU company, note anything he'd need to handle on his side (invoicing as a Partita IVA, W-8BEN for US clients, Deel/Wise rails) — briefly, and only when it's actually load-bearing for that role.

Don't re-tabulate the sheet in chat, and don't pad with encouragement.

## Applying, not just finding

When he asks you to apply — and he does — the search is only the first half. Applying has its own
rules file, and it is not optional reading: **`references/application-rules.md`** holds his
details, his salary number, the standard answers to the questions every ATS asks, the writing
rules, and the list of things you must never do on his behalf. Read it before you touch a form.
Two things in it were learned the hard way: **the CV goes on every single application**, and
**his stated salary range is his, not yours to improve on**.

The workflow that works, per role:

1. **Scout the form** (`agents/form-scout.md`) — one cheap read-only agent per role, in parallel. It reports LIVE / CLOSED / GATED, every required question verbatim, and whether the form is basic or needs writing. This is where most rows die: postings that look live in search are frequently closed, and a real browser is a much stricter test than a fetch or an API read.
2. **Split by what the form wants.** Basic forms — name, email, phone, location, CV, links, dropdowns — get submitted straight away. Forms with written questions need drafted answers first.
3. **Write the material** (`agents/letter-writer.md` + `assets/motivation-letter.md`). Never leave a cover-letter field blank; adapt his real letter to the role. `scripts/make_letter.py` renders it as a PDF in his own layout when the form wants a file.
4. **Submit one at a time** (`agents/applicant.md`). Browser automation doesn't parallelise — concurrent agents fight over tabs. Screenshot the confirmation; if you didn't see one, it didn't happen.
5. **Log it.** Company, role, what went in the judgement-call fields, the verbatim confirmation, the link. Then tell him in chat what you decided for him, so he can correct it before the next batch.

Expect attrition and report it plainly. A sweep of twelve top rows will typically yield a handful
of live basic forms, several that need writing, and several that turn out closed or gated on
work authorisation. That's the market, not a failure of the search — but say so rather than
letting a short list look like laziness.

## Judgment calls

- **"Is this posting any good for me?"** with a single link — skip the sweep entirely. Fetch it, score it against the profile, answer in chat with the honest verdict and what to emphasise if he applies. No spreadsheet unless he asks.
- **A named company** — fetch its board directly (`job-boards.greenhouse.io/<company>`, or an `allowed_domains` search on the company name) instead of running a generic sweep.
- **A repeat run** — if an earlier shortlist exists in this session or in the project, dedupe against it and mark what's new, so he isn't re-reading last week's list. Say how many were carried over.
- **A thin sweep** — if verification leaves only a handful, deliver the handful and say plainly what you'd change next time (different vocabulary, wider geography, contract-only pass). Don't inflate the sheet.
- **He corrects a preference** — a rate expectation, a company he'd never join, a city he would move to — write it into `references/candidate-profile.md` so the next run inherits it.
- **Something in the sweep is worth acting on beyond applying** (a company hiring three roles he fits, a recruiter contact in the posting) — mention it in the chat reply; it's often more valuable than one more row.

## Files in this skill

```
job-hunt/
├── SKILL.md
├── references/
│   ├── candidate-profile.md   — what "good fit" means; keep it current
│   └── sources.md             — tested search playbook, dead ends, verification traps
└── scripts/
    └── build_shortlist.py     — roles JSON → formatted .xlsx shortlist
```

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

Two parallel sweeps: AI/automation/applied-AI across the EU and remote-Europe, and forward-deployed / solutions / implementation / GTM across the EU and UK. Roughly 90 postings opened, 28 returned as verified by the sweeps, 19 actually live when opened in a browser, 12 applications sent.

| Avery | Founding Engineer (Core) | Amsterdam (hybrid) | EUR 3,500-5,000/month, above his stated band. Founder Alisher Jafarov is the contact |
| The Quality Group | AI Engineer (gn) | Germany, remote | **Best stack match of the sweep.** Posting names n8n, Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT Enterprise. No German language requirement. Catch: German residency stated as required |
| Reedsy | AI Engineer | Remote Europe | **Highest pay: EUR 70-120k + 0-0.2% equity.** 5M authors, building a narrative co-pilot. No years bar |
| Spyrosoft | Forward Deployed Engineer (OpenAI) | Poland, fully remote | **Exact target title at his level** — posting says Regular or Senior. PLN 110-150/hr, suits the Partita IVA |
| Hexa (Waniwani) | Forward Deployed Engineer | Europe remote | $8M seed led by Seedcamp. First hire in the function, no years bar. Not a hands-on coding role |
| Nuitée | GTM Engineer | Remote in EU / Barcelona | **Cleanest eligibility line found: "Remote in EU"** with no catch. Profitable pre-$48M Series A led by Accel |
| Pliant | Software Engineer, AI Experience | Remote Germany | No years number; bar is shipping AI features to production |
| HiPeople | Applied AI Engineer | World / Remote | Truly CV-only form. Location field says "World" |
| Jamie | AI Engineer | Remote / Berlin Mitte | **2+ years preferred — lowest bar found all sweep.** Updated 19h before applying |
| (Avery and opus both via join.com, ~2 min each) | | | |

## Needs him, in priority order

1. **Capco Poland** — AI Agent Engineer with Copilot Studio and Power Platform, B2B contract, Krakow hybrid. Live and it is literally his Microsoft certifications as the core requirement. Not submitted because the form asks what he has *built* in Copilot Studio. He holds the Copilot Studio Agent Academy and Power Automate certifications but there is no record of a shipped Copilot Studio solution, and that will not be invented. One answer from him finishes it. https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/capco/jobs/8002464
2. **otonomee x2** (Ireland + Portugal) — blocked on mandatory Internet Provider, Speed Test Download and Upload fields. He runs a speedtest, fills three fields, done. No years bar at all and the stack listed is his CV restated.

- **Greenhouse stale CV** autofilled `Prabhavit_CV-.pdf` from MyGreenhouse at TQG. Remove and re-upload the canonical file every single time.
- **Phone country prefix** at Spyrosoft defaulted to +48 Poland. Switch the country selector first, then type the bare number.

- **CV parsing tool using n8n and Eden AI**; platform for different user profiles

**Qomodo — AI and Low-Code Developer (collaborator)** · Milan · 2024 - Jan 2025
- Figma implementation; dashboard for companies to manage branches

**Get2Germany.com — Lead Developer and Automation Specialist (part time)** · Berlin · Jan-May 2024
- Google API integration; UI/UX Figma to Bubble; database optimisation; **AI automation tools for finding courses, internships and jobs**

**Clubee.com — Low Code Developer and Quality Assurance (full-time, freelance)** · Luxembourg · Sep 2023 - Aug 2024
- Clubee API integration across the frontend; **unit testing and quality assurance**; domain integration, shop and federation dashboard

**Tractionboard.co — Low-Code Developer (internship)** · Utrecht · Aug-Oct 2023
- ChatGPT/OpenAI integration; Figma to Bubble; Sendgrid; responsive design, debugging; Google Ads 4

- **API integration depth** — Office RnD, Nexudus, Clubee, Sendgrid, Google APIs, OpenAI/Anthropic, Eden AI
- **GTM / revenue-adjacent automation** — unusual for an engineer, strong signal for FDE and solutions roles
- **QA as a named function** — Clubee title included Quality Assurance; Playwright on the CV
- **Product ownership** — business logic documentation, coordinating an external agency, PM at Urlink
- **Eight European companies in ~3 years** (UK, Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Luxembourg, Netherlands) — the ramps-fast argument
